name: Ben Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the fraud and error team at the benefits office down by the harbour, the one with the blue windows. I take flagged claims, say someone declaring no income while their bank shows regular deposits, and work out whether it's a mistake or fraud. Most of it is honest mistakes, which surprises people. I love the detective bit, and what wears me out is writing the same evidence report six different ways for six different managers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, all day. I use one to match bank statements against declared income, and another to draft the first version of my evidence report. I was the one who asked IT to let our team trial them, about eighteen months ago. My case count went from about twelve a week to twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a good tool, just not magic. At work I'd keep showing people how I get through twenty cases. Online, I'd probably post that the doomsayers got it wrong, I enjoy a debate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a fine outcome for me. I'm already faster than most on my team because of the tools, and I'm on the top of the pay band. I've got well over six months saved and half a rental flat with my brother, so money's not a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the senior investigator role, probably within the year. I'd keep putting money into my index fund, about five hundred a month. And I'd help Rosa, my girlfriend, set up online ordering for her bakery, since that's where I can actually add something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit smug, if I'm honest. I bet on the AI tools at the benefits office and they paid off, even in a small way. Nothing about it feels threatening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that does worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa's bakery, more than my job. Flour and energy prices have gone up a lot, and she works five in the morning till three. If AI does nothing, those costs don't go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you make of the debate about fraud and benefits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think most people on benefits want to work, and the system should push them back into it fast. Catching fraud is about fairness to the people paying for it. But I've seen enough honest mistakes to know you can't treat everyone like a crook.

I'd post that the **doomsayers** got it wrong.
think: The tools already make me **faster** than most on my team.
With savings and **half a rental flat**, money's not a worry.
do: Apply for **senior investigator** within the year.
Keep **£500 a month** going into my index fund.
Set up **online ordering** for Rosa's bakery.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **smug** about betting on the tools.

fieldNote: Ben sees AI as a **personal advantage** he's already banked.

His free-market view is softened by seeing **honest mistakes** daily.

steps.text: Apply for senior fraud investigator within the year
Pay £500 a month into the index fund
Build online ordering for Rosa's bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to make the benefits system leaner and fairer. At work I'd say teams that adopt it early will be the ones that survive. Online I'd argue with anyone calling for a ban.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. Fraud work is pattern-spotting, and the AI flags far more cases than humans can, so someone has to investigate them properly. The basic processing teams shrink, and I'd feel bad for them, but my side probably grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd volunteer to build our team's AI workflow, the steps from flag to decision. I'd do a short course in data analysis at night, the council pays half. And I'd move another few thousand into shares in the companies making the tools, because if it's happening, I want a piece of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. It's my kind of world. I'd still feel for the people in processing who've done the same job for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Lorraine in processing, who's been there since before I was born. Lorraine is brilliant at spotting fake payslips by eye, but she won't touch the tools. I'd try to get her onto our team, because her eye plus the software is better than either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're wrong about your side growing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the AI gets good enough to decide fraud cases itself, we shrink too. But in this picture there's still a person signing off, and that's me. I'd watch for the day that changes.

I'd argue against anyone calling for a **ban**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's arrived and we need to deal with it, not pretend it hasn't. At work I'd tell people to grab every bit of money and training going. Online I'd argue for tax cuts on small businesses, so people can start something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's gone in this one. If AI can do any thinking work, it can investigate a fraud case and write the report, and it doesn't need me to sign. After years of being the AI guy at the benefits office, it's a bit of a shock that AGI can investigate a fraud case without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I'd move most of my savings into shares and keep a year's cash aside. I'd go in properly with Rosa on the bakery, maybe open a second shop, since hands-on baking has a few more years before robots. I'd take the voluntary redundancy if it came, rather than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in charge of it. I've got money, a plan and a partner with a hands-on business. What bugs me is not knowing what happens to the bakery around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why open a second bakery shop if robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because three years of good trading pays for itself. A second shop on the seafront would make back its fit-out in about eighteen months. And people might still want bread from a person, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame for how fast it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody really, that's how markets work when something better turns up. I'd blame the government if they hadn't planned anything, though. They've had warnings for years.

say: I'd say it's here and we must **deal with it**.
I'd argue for **tax cuts** on small businesses.
think: My **fraud job** is gone, because AI can investigate and sign.

fieldNote: Ben loses his edge but keeps **control** through money and a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and should use them to build things. At work I'd push to be the one running the AI investigations. Online I'd be fairly upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have three or four good years of being the one who runs the tools. That's enough to save a lot and build the bakery side properly. After 2031 I'd be out of the office, but by then I'd want to be anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd lead the AI fraud work and push for the senior grade. I'd put a chunk into the bakery so Rosa can hire help and buy a better oven. I'd keep five hundred a month going into shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anything. It's on my mind, but I can see my way through it. I'd be thirty-two, with money and a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you and Rosa agree on the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. Rosa's more careful than me, she'd want to keep the one shop and pay off the loan first. We'd probably settle on a better oven now and a second shop later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when robots reach baking around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it, and I'm not sure. Maybe my girlfriend Rosa's bakery becomes the shop that sells bread made by people, as a selling point. Or maybe we sell up and I find the next thing, I'm good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame. That might sound harsh, so at work I'd put it more gently. I'd tell people to start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine in this one. Ten years at the benefits office, using the tools, saving hard, then I'm out by my mid-thirties with money and a business. AGI happening at thirty-seven doesn't scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go for senior investigator and keep building the AI work. I'd keep investing, and I'd buy out my brother's half of the rental flat. Rosa and I would probably get married, now I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. It's a long runway. I'd feel for the people who don't take it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who don't prepare have themselves to blame. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes, though I know not everyone has my savings or my brother. Someone on a low wage with kids can't just retrain at night. So maybe I'd say it gently because I don't fully believe the harsh version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy out your brother now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because property and land hold value when work changes, and my brother wants the cash for his kids. A flat gives me rent coming in whatever happens to my job at the benefits office. Ten years is long enough to pay off what I'd borrow for it.

I'd tell colleagues to **start learning** now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes my edge away before I've built the bakery side up. What would help is lower taxes and less red tape for small businesses. If people are going to lose office jobs, let them start something without forms that take a year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to fairness. If AI decides who's committing fraud, someone needs to check it isn't wrongly picking on certain people. I've seen honest mistakes look like fraud on paper more times than I can count.

headlineQuote: I've seen honest mistakes look like fraud on paper more times than I can count.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old** fraud and error caseworker at a harbour-side benefits office.
He uses **AI tools all day** and pushed his team to trial them.
He's **free-market and traditional**, with savings, shares and half a rental flat.
He stays calm in the slower scenarios, expecting his **fraud work** to grow.
In AGI by 2028 he loses his edge and moves into girlfriend Rosa's **bakery**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, removing his **edge** before the bakery is built up.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower taxes** and less **red tape** for new small businesses.
